lessons.title: 01 From lattices to the 230 space groups
lessons.summary: Distinguish what 7,14,32,230 count, then understand why 230 is not 14×32.
objectives: Distinguish lattice, basis, and the actual crystal's space group
Explain the hierarchy of 7 crystal systems, 14 Bravais types, and 230  space group  types
Distinguish the 65 Sohncke types from the 11 enantiomorphic pairs of space-group types

sections.title: Periodicity and local structure jointly determine symmetry
paragraphs: Placing the same atomic motif at every translation-lattice point creates a periodic structure. The translation lattice records repetition only; chemical species, relative positions, and magnetic moments may reduce structural symmetry further. A cube-shaped cell alone does not establish a cubic  space group .

Three-dimensional crystals have 7 crystal systems, 14 Bravais-lattice types and 32 crystallographic point-group types. Space groups additionally retain translations, screws and glides, giving 230 types under crystallographic conventions. Symbols such as P, I, F and C express a lattice in a particular conventional cell; the same lattice can use different bases, and lattice letters cannot be combined arbitrarily with every crystal system.

sections.title: 230 counts types, not operations
paragraphs: Every actual  space group  contains infinitely many lattice translations and thus infinitely many elements. A finite database operation list contains representatives modulo translations. For a centered  conventional cell  reduced only modulo integer-cell translations, the list also contains centering-translation representatives, so its row count need not equal the point  group order .

The numbers are grouped by crystal system: triclinic 1–2, monoclinic 3–15, orthorhombic 16–74, tetragonal 75–142, trigonal 143–167, hexagonal 168–194 and cubic 195–230; the respective counts are 2, 13, 59, 68, 25, 27 and 36.

sections.title: Chiral structures and enantiomorphic group types are different counts
paragraphs: The 65 Sohncke types contain only orientation-preserving spatial operations and permit  chirality  crystal structures. Among them, 22  space group  types form 11 enantiomorphic pairs, such as P4₁（76） and P4₃（78）. Other Sohncke types still accommodate  chirality  structures but have no separately numbered enantiomorphic group type.

If classification permits orientation-reversing affine coordinate changes and merges each enantiomorphic pair, the 230 types become 219 affine types. The equivalence relation has changed; no space-group table has omitted 11 groups.

example.title: Choose among P4, P4₁, and P4₃
steps: P4（75）, P4₁（76）, and P4₃（78） all have fourfold point symmetry, with rotational parts belonging to  point group  4.
P4₁ translates by c/4 along its axis with every 90° rotation; P4₃ translates by 3c/4 per 90° rotation.
Compare screw handedness along a fixed positive axis: 76 and 78 form a pair. Point group 4 alone cannot distinguish them.
example.result: point group  retains directional symmetry;  space group  also retains the accompanying  fractional translation  of each operation.

lessons.pitfall: 230 counts space-group types of three-dimensional periodic crystals; it does not count unit-cell shapes and does not include all quasicrystalline symmetry types.

quiz.question: Why do P4₁ and P4₃ have different space-group numbers despite sharing point group 4?
choices: Their screw translations along the axis and their handedness differ
One has infinitely many elements; the other has only four
quiz.explanation: Both have  point group  4. In the same positive-axis convention, their screw translations are c/4 and 3c/4, forming enantiomorphic  space group  types.

quiz.question: How many affine types result from merging each of the 11 enantiomorphic pairs among the 230 space-group types?
quiz.explanation: Merging each pair reduces the count by one, so 230−11=219; do not subtract 22.

lessons.title: 02 Compose spatial actions with Seitz operators
lessons.summary: A translation following a rotation is carried along by the next rotation; multiplication order must be retained.
objectives: Derive the composition formula from x′=Rx+t
Work out an operation’s inverse by hand
Distinguish unfolded coordinates from coordinates modulo the cell

sections.title: First fix coordinates and action direction
paragraphs: This course uses fractional-coordinate column vectors x. The active operation g={R|t} sends an atom to x′=Rx+t. AB means B acts first, then A. In a fractional basis, R need not satisfy the ordinary relation RᵀR=I; checking an isometry also requires the lattice metric.
For two successive operations, the later rotation also rotates the earlier displacement. Translation parts therefore cannot always be added directly.

sections.title: Inverse operations and folding into the lattice
paragraphs: Demanding that the inverse map Rx+t back to x gives the inverse rotation matrix and a rotated negative translation. This formula applies to rotations, screws, mirrors and glides alike.

Plots often wrap each coordinate component into [0,1) to show equivalent points in one cell. The discarded integer translations still contribute Bloch phases; coincidence in a real-space picture does not imply identical wavefunction operators.

example.title: Why do rotations and translations fail to commute?
steps: Apply B then A: AB={C₂z|(−1/2,0,0)}.
A followed by B: BA={C₂z|(1/2,0,0)}; the two results differ by a lattice translation along x.
For the origin, the unwrapped coordinates are (−1/2,0,0) and (1/2,0,0), respectively; they coincide only after wrapping into the unit cell.
example.result: Wrapped plots can coincide, but the original Seitz operations and their k-dependent phases must remain distinct.

lessons.pitfall: R₁t₂ in the composition formula cannot be shortened to t₂. Reducing modulo integers before completing the algebra may also erase required translation phases.

quiz.question: For A={R|t} and B={S|u}, what is the translation part of AB?
quiz.explanation: ABx=R(Sx+u)+t=RSx+Ru+t, so the translation part is Ru+t.

quiz.question: Which is the inverse operation of {R|t}?
quiz.explanation: Applying {R⁻¹|−R⁻¹t} to Rx+t returns exactly x. Only in special cases can −R⁻¹t be simplified to −t.

lessons.title: 03  screw axis ,  glide plane , and  fractional translation
lessons.summary: Repeat a composite operation to see when it restores the same orientation and how far it translates through the lattice.
objectives: Calculate repeated action of an nₚ screw
Distinguish squares of mirrors and glides
Identify symmorphic and nonsymmorphic space groups with an origin-independent definition

sections.title: A full rotation need not restore spatial position
paragraphs: An nₚ screw along z rotates by 2π/n and translates along its axis by p/n axial lattice periods. After n operations, orientation returns but position shifts by p periods.

For example, squaring 2₁ gives a full lattice translation; applying 4₁ four times also gives a full lattice translation. Here the “period” refers to complete, unwrapped coordinates, not merely coincidence within one cell.

sections.title: A glide does more than reflect
paragraphs: A mirror m plus  fractional translation  τ parallel to its plane forms glide g={m|τ}. Since mτ=τ, applying it twice gives {I|2τ}. A perpendicular translation mainly changes the mirror's position and cannot directly be treated as intrinsic glide translation.

A symmorphic space group admits an origin at which each point-group coset has a representative with zero translation, so G=T⋊P. A nonsymmorphic group cannot achieve this simultaneously. Fractional t in one table alone is inconclusive: shifting the origin, using a centered conventional cell and choosing representatives all change the apparent notation.
sections.formula: {m|τ}²={I|mτ+τ}={I|2τ}, with τ parallel to the mirror

example.title: 2₁ screw along z
steps: Take R=diag(−1,−1,1) and t=(0,0,1/2), consistent with this site’s BC setting for SG 4 and its experiment panel.
Starting from x=(0.2,0.3,0.1), one application gives (−0.2,−0.3,0.6).
Applying it again gives (0.2,0.3,1.1), differing from the starting point by (0,0,1).
Wrapping the result into [0,1) returns to the starting point; retaining unwrapped coordinates reveals a full c translation.
example.result: 2₁ has a two-step cycle in a point plot modulo translations, but the full operator satisfies g²=T(c).

lessons.pitfall: “A screw/glide expression exists” is not equivalent to “ space group  must be nonsymmorphic” for arbitrary cells and representatives. Check whether allowed origin and representative choices can remove this  fractional translation .

quiz.question: What is the full spatial operation after applying a 4₁ screw along c four times?
quiz.explanation: Four 90° rotations restore orientation, while four c/4 translations add to c.

quiz.question: m is the xy mirror, τ=(1/2,0,0). What is {m|τ}²?
quiz.explanation: m²=I and an in-plane translation satisfies mτ=τ, so the square is {I|2τ}.

lessons.title: 04 Orbits, site symmetry, and Wyckoff positions
lessons.summary: The same group can generate different numbers of equivalent positions at general and special points.
objectives: Generate point orbits modulo translation using group operations
Explain why the orbit shrinks as  stabilizer  grows
Distinguish orbit calculation from complete Wyckoff-letter assignment

sections.title: First ask which operations fix this point
paragraphs: The orbit of x contains all Rx+t; an intracell orbit also reduces modulo the chosen cell translations. Operations fixing the actual spatial point form the  site-symmetry group . For a finite  quotient group  action, points differing by a cell translation are identified, and  stabilizer  is calculated within the same  quotient group .

For a finite-group action, orbit size times stabilizer size equals group order. Use a consistent cell and translation subgroup: conventional-cell and primitive-cell multiplicities may differ by a centering factor.
sections.formula: |Orb(x)| × |Stab(x)| = |Ḡ|, where Ḡ is the finite operation group used for this reduction

sections.title: A  Wyckoff position  is an entire class of orbits
paragraphs: General positions have no additional site symmetry; special positions satisfy coordinate constraints that make some equivalent points coincide. Wyckoff letters name families of orbits with the same type of site symmetry and must be read together with the space-group number, cell setting and origin.

Generating an orbit answers which positions are equivalent. Full Wyckoff identification also requires matching standard coordinate parameters and site symmetry; multiplicity alone does not uniquely determine a letter. For decimal approximations, tolerance also affects whether a point lies at a special position.

example.title: A general point and inversion center in P−1
steps: In P−1 (2), choose the origin as an inversion center. Modulo primitive translations, the operations are E and i.
x=(0.2,0.3,0.4) generates (0.2,0.3,0.4) and (0.8,0.7,0.6); the orbit size is 2 and stabilizer size 1.
x=(0,0,0) is inversion invariant; orbit size drops to 1 while  stabilizer  size becomes 2.
Other half-integer positions can also have inversion site symmetry; equal multiplicity alone does not assign them the same Wyckoff letter.
example.result: Both positions satisfy orbit–stabilizer: 2=2×1=1×2.

lessons.pitfall: “Two equivalent points” is not a Wyckoff name. Site symmetry, orbit multiplicity, and the Wyckoff letter are related but distinct information.

quiz.question: A general point in P−1 modulo primitive translations has a two-point orbit. What happens when it moves to an inversion center?
choices: The orbit still contains two distinct points
The orbit becomes one point and  stabilizer  grows
quiz.explanation: Changing the position under study does not change the specified group. An inversion center is fixed by E and i, shrinking its orbit to 1 and increasing its stabilizer to 2.

quiz.question: Can orbit multiplicity alone uniquely determine a Wyckoff letter?
choices: Only if the multiplicity is even
No; group, setting, coordinates, and site symmetry must also be checked
quiz.explanation: One group may have several  Wyckoff position  with equal multiplicity, and letters also depend on the standard setting.

lessons.title: 05 Little groups of k and nonsymmorphic Bloch phases
lessons.summary: The same crystal needs different small representations at different k points; screw translations enter eigenvalues.
objectives: Test the little-group condition with reciprocal-space transformations
Write the Bloch phase for active translation
Derive screw eigenvalues at Γ and the boundary from the square of 2₁

sections.title: Not every spatial operation preserves k
paragraphs: When real-space fractional coordinates transform by R, reciprocal coordinates transform by R⁻ᵀ. The little group Gₖ retains operations sending k to k+K, where K is a reciprocal vector. Gₖ includes all lattice translations; taking only rotational parts gives the finite little co-group.

For a centered  conventional cell , K must be a genuine  reciprocal lattice  vector; arbitrary integer triples cannot unconditionally be treated as equivalent. If textbooks and software use different  primitive cell  or row-vector conventions, matrix expressions must also be converted.

sections.title: Translations survive as phases
paragraphs: This course uses T(t)ψ(r)=ψ(r−t). For ψₖ(r)=exp(2πik·r)uₖ(r), a lattice translation L gives T(L)ψₖ=exp(−2πik·L)ψₖ. Here k is in fractional reciprocal coordinates, so the dot product has no additional unit factor.

After selecting little-co-group representatives gR, their product may differ from another representative by a lattice translation L. The small representation then carries exp(−2πik·L). This is the k-space algebraic information of nonsymmorphic structure; deleting t from every operation loses it.

example.title: The eigenvalues of a 2₁ screw depend on k
steps: Choose the z-axis screw g={C₂z|c/2}, in this site's BC setting of SG 4. Along its invariant k line, single-valued representations satisfy g²=T(c).
Screw eigenvalue λ therefore satisfies λ²=exp(−2πik_z), namely λ=±exp(−πik_z).
At Γ, k_z=0 gives λ=±1; at k=(0,0,1/2), λ=±i. The sets of positive and negative eigenvalues are consistent with the phase convention.
This derives only screw eigenvalues. Paired energy degeneracy also depends on other spatial or antiunitary symmetries.
example.result: fractional translation  makes boundary representations differ from a direct application of ordinary  point group  tables.

lessons.pitfall: Identical k-point names do not guarantee identical reciprocal-coordinate bases; complex eigenvalues of one screw alone do not prove twofold degeneracy of every level.

quiz.question: With this lesson's phase convention, what is the Bloch phase for translation by c at k=(0,0,1/2)?
quiz.explanation: exp(−2πi×1/2)=−1. A full lattice translation along c still acts as a nontrivial phase here.

quiz.question: If a spinless 2₁ screw satisfies λ²=−1, what are its possible eigenvalues?
quiz.explanation: Both i and −i square to −1. Additional symmetry must be checked to decide whether these eigenvalue sectors pair at equal energy.

lessons.title: 06 Standard cells, BC labels, and calculation records
lessons.summary: Make the idea of the “same group” reproducible by specifying the basis, origin, k coordinates and representation labels.
objectives: Transform operations consistently when changing basis and shifting the origin
Distinguish specific BC and Bilbao/ITA settings
Use complete calculation records to explain when representation labels are comparable

sections.title: A coordinate change preserves the structure but changes its matrices
paragraphs: Let old and new coordinates obey x_old=P x_new+p. Columns of P give new basis vectors in the old basis, and p is the new origin in old coordinates. Substituting into the spatial operation transforms rotation and translation together.

Reciprocal coordinates must become k_new =Pᵀk old to preserve k·x phase pairing. Do not rotate atoms while retaining old k values. Switching between  conventional cell  and  primitive cell  also requires checking changes in translation lattice and atom count.

sections.title: Save number, setting, and labels together
paragraphs: An international  space group  number identifies a group type, not every axis order, origin, or operation list. Standard Bilbao/ITA settings and Bradley–Cracknell (BC) representation settings differ for some groups. Use the site's existing conversion and labeling tools and first check their returned transformations and conventions.

Standard representation labels such as Γ₁ depend on the group, k star, setting and labeling rules. Temporary numerical labels D1 and D2 identify results from this calculation only; their order does not establish a BC or Bilbao label. Record the basis for the mapping, phase convention and double-valued setting.

example.title: Shift the coordinate origin of inversion
steps: In old coordinates, inversion is R=−I, t=0. Keep basis P=I and place the new origin at old coordinate p=(1/4,0,0).
Substituting into t_new=(−I)p−p gives (−1/2,0,0).
Modulo lattice translation this can be written (1/2,0,0), but retaining the full transformation helps track representation phases.
Inversion in the new coordinates remains the same physical operation, but its center no longer lies at the new origin.
example.result: A 1/2 in the translation column does not imply that a physical half-translation has been added to the structure.

lessons.pitfall: Standard-label mapping does not mean renaming D1 alphabetically. Align operations, k, bases, and phases before comparing settings.

quiz.question: For x_old =P x new+p, how must reciprocal coordinates transform to preserve phase pairing?
quiz.explanation: k_old·P x_new=(Pᵀk_old)·x_new; shifting the origin contributes only a coordinate-independent phase.

quiz.question: Can a numerical D1 be identified as BC Γ₁ merely because it appears first?
choices: Yes; every program uses the same order
No; a justified mapping to standard labels is required
quiz.explanation: Several representations may have equal dimensions, and numerical order is not fixed. Compare operations,  character , or matrices in the same setting using an explicit mapping rule.

lessons.title: 07 Why must an electron spinor rotate through 4π?
lessons.summary: One  spatial rotation  corresponds to two spinor matrices; the 2π minus sign can appear in coherent comparisons.
objectives: Calculate spin-1/2 rotation matrices
Compare spatial vectors, spinor amplitudes, and probabilities
Explain the difference between an overall minus sign and an observable relative phase

sections.title: Vector rotations and spinor rotations
paragraphs: SO(3) describes orientation-preserving rotations in three dimensions; SU(2) matrices act on two-component spin-1/2 spinors. Each SO(3) rotation has two preimages U and −U in SU(2): the double cover.

For an active rotation through θ about unit axis n, this lesson uses U=exp(−iθn·σ/2). A 2π rotation gives U=−I; only 4π returns to I. This minus sign acts on the whole spinor and does not reverse the magnetic-moment arrow.

sections.title: When can the minus sign be compared?
paragraphs: An isolated pure state ψ and −ψ represent the same quantum ray, with identical probability density, norm, and spin expectations. Magnetic-moment arrows alone therefore cannot reveal the difference between 2π and 4π.

If only one of two coherent paths undergoes a spinor rotation, its minus sign becomes a phase relative to the other path and may change the interference output. The displayed real/imaginary parts and reference-state overlaps record this algebraic distinction; they do not imply direct measurement of a single overall phase.

example.title: Rotate |↑⟩ about z
steps: A measurement of z spin at every step still yields up, and the state norm remains 1.
Use the interactive panel to see the spatial rotation needed for the complex amplitude to complete one turn in the complex plane.
example.result: One spatial turn gives half a phase cycle of the spinor; two spatial turns fully restore the chosen amplitude.

lessons.pitfall: A spinor’s sign change after 2π does not mean “negative electron probability” or “reversed spin direction”; distinguish global phase from relative interference phase.

quiz.question: What is U(n,2π) for spin 1/2?
quiz.explanation: cosπ=−1, sinπ=0, so the rotation matrix is −I and probabilities and norm are unchanged.

quiz.question: What may be observed if only one coherent path undergoes a 2π spin rotation?
choices: The path probability must be negative
A change in interference phase relative to the unrotated reference path
quiz.explanation: For one path the 2π factor −1 is an overall phase; between two coherent paths it becomes a comparable relative phase.

lessons.title: 08 A double group does more than duplicate the old table
lessons.summary: The new central element changes multiplication: the lift of an ordinary twofold rotation has order four.
objectives: Understand the action of central element Ē
Test double-group multiplication using a lift of C₂
Distinguish double-group element counts, conjugacy-class counts, and representation dimensions

sections.title: Retain the 2π rotation as an element
paragraphs: Let Ē denote the central element that covers the ordinary identity rotation but acts on spinors as −I. It satisfies Ē²=E and commutes with all elements. Each ordinary operation R has two lifts, R̃ and ĒR̃.

A finite point group's double group has twice as many elements, but its numbers of conjugacy classes and irreducible representations need not double. The two lifts of an original conjugacy class can form one class or split into two; lifts of distinct original classes cannot merge. Choosing one lift per operation usually does not give a closed half: two “unbarred” lifts can multiply into the other half.

sections.title: Checking squares reveals the changed multiplication
paragraphs: Ordinary C₂ satisfies C₂²=E, whereas its spinor lift C̃₂ squares to Ē rather than E. A double group therefore cannot generally be interpreted as the direct product of the ordinary group with an independent binary switch.

For groups with inversion or mirrors, lifts of improper operations to spin space must also be specified. Standard crystallographic double groups usually take inversion squared as E and a mirror lift squared as Ē. The SU(2) formula for SO(3) does not uniquely prescribe every O(3) operation.

example.title: The  double group  of C₂ is a cyclic group of order four
steps: Take C̃₂z=−iσ_z=diag(−i,i).
Its square is −I, corresponding to Ē; its cube is −C̃₂z and its fourth power is I.
The four elements are E, C̃₂z, Ē, and ĒC̃₂z, with multiplication structure C₄.
Incorrectly duplicating C₂ into C₂×C₂ would make every nonidentity element have order two, contradicting the order-four element just calculated.
example.result: A double group requires actual lifted multiplication; adding a label without changing multiplication is insufficient.

lessons.pitfall: “Twice as many elements” implies neither “twice every  conjugacy class ” nor “twice every energy level.” This lesson concerns group structure; energy degeneracies additionally depend on representations and antiunitary conditions.

quiz.question: What is the square of the spinor lift C̃₂z=−iσ_z?
quiz.explanation: (−iσ_z)²=(−i)²σ_z²=−I; only four applications give I.

quiz.question: An ordinary finite  point group  has order h and its double  group order  order 2h. Does this imply twice as many  irreducible representation ?
choices: Yes; every row can simply be duplicated
No; the count depends on the double group's conjugacy classes
No, because  double group  has no  irreducible representation
quiz.explanation: The number of irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes. The two sets of lifts of an original conjugacy class may form one class or split into two; classes are not mechanically duplicated.

references.chapter: §I–II, double-group elements and lifts of improper rotations

lessons.title: 09  double-valued representation  and  spin–orbit coupling
lessons.summary: First take the tensor product of orbital and spin representations, then decompose it into double-group irreducible representations; SOC does not automatically produce twofold degeneracy.
objectives: Distinguish single- and double-valued sectors by the sign of D(Ē)
Calculate the spin-1/2 rotation  character
Explain what representation decomposition can and cannot predict with SOC

sections.title: Double-valued refers to the central element's sign
paragraphs: double group  itself has ordinary linear representations. If Ē is represented by +I, the representation descends to a  single-valued representation  of the original group. If Ē is represented by −I, it is a  double-valued representation  in the usual terminology. Double-valued does not require dimension two. For example, C₂  double group  has one-dimensional  double-valued representation  with C̃₂→±i.

The complete irreducible representations of a finite double group obey the sum-of-squared-dimensions rule for its order. If the workbench displays only the double-valued sector, neither its row count nor its sum of squared dimensions checks the completeness of the entire double group.
sections.formula: Single-valued sector: D(Ē)=+I; double-valued sector: D(Ē)=−I

sections.title: From orbital×spin to allowed  multiplet
paragraphs: For an applicable nonmagnetic reference model, take the tensor product of the orbital representation Γorb with the spin-1/2 representation; the SOC Hamiltonian must respect the combined double-group action. Reducing that tensor product identifies which irreducible subspaces may split apart and their symmetry dimensions.

For rotation angle θ, the spin-1/2 character is 2cos(θ/2). Tensor-product characters multiply those of the factors. Group theory constrains allowed block structure but does not alone give SOC splitting magnitudes, energy ordering, or real material parameters.

example.title: Three-dimensional p orbitals and spin 1/2
steps: In the spherically symmetric atomic limit, l=1 p orbitals supply 3 orbital states; multiplying by 2 spin states gives dimension 6.
Angular-momentum addition gives j=1/2 and j=3/2, of dimensions 2+4=6.
In a crystal, restrict these states to the particular  double group  and reexamine its  irreducible representation .
Changing crystal-field or SOC parameters can change energy splittings but cannot violate the transformation laws required within the same symmetry subspace.
example.result: Tensor-product dimension is conserved. Labels and degeneracies in a particular crystal must be assessed using its group and time reversal.

lessons.pitfall: The 2+4 split here is spherical angular-momentum coupling; p states in every crystal need not form those same two levels. Temporary labels such as D1 are not standard  double group  labels either.

quiz.question: If a representation has D(Ē)=−I, which statement is most accurate?
choices: It belongs to the double-valued sector
quiz.explanation: The central minus sign defines the double-valued sector, whose dimension can be one or larger. Time reversal is a separate condition to add explicitly.

quiz.question: What is the rotation  character  for spin 1/2 rotated by π about any axis?
quiz.explanation: χspin(π)=2cos(π/2)=0. The matrix itself remains a nonzero unitary matrix; only its trace vanishes.

references.chapter: §III, double-group representations

lessons.title: 10 Conditions for time reversal and Kramers pairing
lessons.summary: Antiunitarity, the same momentum subspace, and a square of −I are all essential.
objectives: Correctly square Θ=−iσ_yK
Determine the k point to which  time reversal  sends a state
Distinguish the Bloch-level constraints from Θ alone and from PΘ

sections.title: Antiunitarity does not mean negative norm
paragraphs: K denotes  complex conjugation  in the selected basis. For spin 1/2, choose Θ=−iσ_yK; changing its overall phase does not alter its physical action. Θ is an antilinear norm-preserving operator, Θ(cψ)=c*Θψ.
Writing Θ=UK gives Θ²=UU*, not U². For U=−iσ_y here, Θ²=−I. Squaring to −I does not mean norms are not preserved: an antiunitary operator still satisfies ⟨Θψ|Θφ⟩=⟨φ|ψ⟩.

sections.title: An equal-energy partner need not lie at the same k
paragraphs: If the Hamiltonian preserves an antiunitary A, A maps the current state space to itself, and A²=−I, every eigenstate has an orthogonal equal-energy partner: the Kramers result. Θ alone maps k to −k. At generic k it relates spectra at two momenta, rather than automatically ensuring double degeneracy at one k.

At a time-reversal-invariant momentum (TRIM), −k=k+K. If Θ is indeed a symmetry and Θ²=−I, it pairs states at the same k. If ordinary inversion P is also present, commutes with Θ and satisfies P²=I, then PΘ preserves every k and squares to −I, protecting twofold degeneracy throughout the Brillouin zone. Magnetic groups may contain other antiunitary combinations; test each individually.

example.title: Compare k=0, k=0.2, and k=1/2
steps: For example, for one-dimensional  reciprocal lattice   fractional coordinates , Θ maps them to 0,−0.2,−1/2, respectively.
0 equals itself, and −1/2 differs from 1/2 by a reciprocal-lattice vector; both are TRIM.
0.2 and −0.2 are inequivalent; time reversal requires only equal-energy partners at those two momenta.
If PΘ satisfying these conditions is also present, pairing within the same k subspace is possible at 0.2 as well.
example.result: First test whether the operation returns to the same k, then test its square; enabling SOC alone does not establish degeneracy.

lessons.pitfall: Zero net moment, SOC, or being at a TRIM cannot individually replace checking that an antiunitary symmetry actually exists and squares to −I.

quiz.question: For a spin-1/2 crystal preserving Θ, what does Θ alone guarantee when generic k and −k are inequivalent?
choices: Every band at the same k must be twofold degenerate
Every band must be fourfold degenerate
quiz.explanation: Θ connects subspaces at two different momenta. Same-k degeneracy follows directly only when the operation returns to the same k or an additional antiunitary operation preserves k.

quiz.question: If A=UK is antiunitary, how is its square calculated?
quiz.explanation: KU=U*K, hence UKUK=UU*K²=UU*; complex conjugation is essential.

lessons.title: 11 Why is a magnetic moment a time-reversal-odd axial vector?
lessons.summary: The same mirror acts differently on displacement and magnetic moment; a primed operation must additionally reverse the moment.
objectives: Transform atomic positions, polar vectors and axial-vector magnetic moments separately
Explain the difference between spatial inversion and time reversal
Determine whether an operation preserves the entire magnetic structure

sections.title: Positions and magnetic moments are separate datasets
paragraphs: A spatial operation first maps atomic positions to Rx+t. A time-even polar vector v, such as displacement, becomes Rv. A magnetic moment m is a time-odd axial vector and becomes det(R)Rm in orthonormal Cartesian coordinates. Inversion reverses a polar vector but preserves an axial magnetic moment.

time reversal  Θ preserves positions and reverses magnetic moments. A primed spatial operation has ε=1; an unprimed one has ε=0, with the additional factor (−1)^ε. If R uses a nonorthogonal fractional basis, convert it to Cartesian form before applying this expression to Cartesian moments. Time-odd polar vectors such as velocity also require the  time reversal  sign; the time-even displacement-v formula here does not apply to them.
sections.formula: x′=Rx+t; v′=Rv (time-even polar vector); m′=(−1)^ε det(R)Rm

sections.title: Symmetry must match the entire structure
paragraphs: To test structural invariance, check that every atom maps to the same species and its moment matches the target-site moment. Checking the total moment alone is insufficient: a  antiferromagnetic  structure may have zero total moment while pure  time reversal  sends it to a different magnetic domain.

This course uses the corresponding spin and spatial transformations of the magnetic-space-group framework. Without SOC, larger independent spin-rotation symmetries may arise; these are spin-group questions and cannot be identified directly with the 1651 magnetic space groups discussed here.

example.title: An xy mirror acts differently on the two kinds of arrows
steps: Take mirror R=diag(1,1,−1), det(R)=−1.
For the polar vector v=(1,2,3), v′=(1,2,−3).
For an unprimed magnetic moment m=(1,2,3), m′=(−1,−2,3).
For the primed mirror m′, additionally apply  time reversal ; the resulting moment is (1,2,−3).
example.result: A prime changes the transformation of magnetic moments, not the spatial mirror’s action on atomic positions.

lessons.pitfall: A magnetic moment is not an ordinary displacement arrow. Omitting det(R), especially for mirrors and inversion, gives incorrect magnetic symmetry.

quiz.question: How does pure  spatial inversion  R=−I act on moment m?
quiz.explanation: det(−I)=−1, so det(R)Rm=(−1)(−I)m=m. Time reversal is what reverses the magnetic moment.

quiz.question: Does zero total moment in an antiferromagnetic structure establish pure time reversal as a symmetry?
choices: Yes, because the moment sum is unchanged
No; magnetic moments must match site by site
Yes, if all atoms are identical
quiz.explanation: A zero sum does not mean each site's moment is unchanged.  time reversal  may map ordered structure to another magnetic domain; inspect the full moment distribution.

lessons.title: 12 Four categories of  magnetic space group  and 1651 types
lessons.summary: Distinguish types I–IV by the presence of pure time reversal, pure antitranslations and the translation lattice of the unitary subgroup.
objectives: Identify the four magnetic-space-group types from their operation structure
Remember type counts without treating types as names of magnetic orders
Distinguish magnetic cells from chemical cells defined without magnetic order

sections.title: First isolate the subgroup H without time reversal
paragraphs: Type I contains only ordinary spatial operations, M=H, with 230 types. Type II, the gray groups, adds a time-reversed partner to every ordinary space-group operation: M=H∪ΘH, also 230 types. Pure Θ is a symmetry in type II.

Types III and IV contain  antiunitary operation  but no pure Θ. They can be written M=H∪aH, where H is a unitary index-two subgroup and a an antiunitary representative. Classification must additionally inspect translations, rather than merely count primes in a table.

sections.title: Types III and IV differ in their translation lattices
paragraphs: Removing every prime gives the ordinary family space group F. For type III, H and F share a translation lattice, while the point group of H has index 2 in that of F. There are 674 types.

Type IV contains antitranslation a=ΘT(τ), where τ is not a translation of H but 2τ is. H's translation lattice has index 2 relative to F, and both share the same  point group . There are 517 types. A magnetic cell is determined by unitary translations preserving full magnetic order and may exceed the chemical cell defined without that order.

These are symmetry classifications, not one-to-one synonyms for ferromagnetism, antiferromagnetism and paramagnetism. Pure Θ in type II excludes static local-moment order; classifying a particular magnetic structure still requires checking positions and moments.

example.title: An alternating ↑↓ chain
steps: Let chemical repetition distance be a, with moments up on even sites and down on odd sites.
T(a) alone exchanges ↑ and ↓ and does not preserve the magnetic order; Θ alone does not preserve it either.
ΘT(a) exchanges positions and reverses moments, restoring the order; T(2a) is a unitary translation.
In a suitable three-dimensional periodic extension, this antitranslation is a typical type-IV mechanism. The one-dimensional schematic alone does not specify a unique three-dimensional BNS number.
example.result: τ=a is a half-translation of the magnetic unit cell; a combined symmetry can survive while both component operations are separately broken.

lessons.pitfall: Magnetism does not necessarily imply type III, nor does zero net moment select type IV. The complete operation set determines the type.

quiz.question: Which category of  magnetic space group  must contain pure  time reversal  Θ?
quiz.explanation: For type II, M=H∪ΘH; choosing the identity in H gives pure Θ. The definitions of types III and IV exclude pure Θ.

quiz.question: In a type-IV antitranslation ΘT(τ), how is τ related to the unitary translation lattice?
choices: τ itself must be a unitary translation
τ is not a unitary translation, but 2τ is
2τ cannot be a unitary translation either
quiz.explanation: An antitranslation's spatial part is a half-translation relative to the unitary translation lattice. Squaring restores a unitary lattice translation; electronic spinors may additionally contribute a central minus sign.

lessons.title: 13 BNS, OG, and the 122 magnetic point groups
lessons.summary: Read magnetic-group numbers and settings correctly before deciding which spatial information  magnetic point group  omits.
objectives: Distinguish BNS/OG labels from equivalence of physical groups
Explain the origin of 122=32+32+58
Explain why  magnetic point group  cannot recover all antitranslation information

sections.title: Interpret numbers together with their cell settings
paragraphs: BNS and OG are two standard description systems for the same magnetic space groups. BNS commonly uses two-part numbers and OG three-part numbers. These are identifiers, not decimals, and cannot be converted by string substitution or arithmetic.

Particularly for type IV, the two systems often use different cells and group-family organizations. Conversion tables must be accompanied by basis, origin, and operation transformations; atomic positions, moment components, and reciprocal coordinates must transform consistently. Replacing one number by another does not automatically convert a structure.

sections.title: The 122 magnetic point groups classify a different level
paragraphs: Ignoring spatial translations while retaining rotations and time-reversal marks gives a magnetic point group. Three-dimensional crystallographic magnetic point groups comprise 32 types without antiunitary operations, 32 gray types, and 58 black-and-white types: 122 total.

Ignoring translations turns type-IV ΘT(τ) into Θ, so an ordered  antiferromagnetic  can have a gray  magnetic point group . This does not contradict “a type-II  magnetic space group  contains pure Θ”: the former has already discarded the crucial half-translation when taking the  point group .

Magnetic point groups constrain uniform macroscopic tensors, but magnetic space groups are needed for k-dependent phases, antitranslations or magnetic-cell information. The totals of 1651 magnetic space groups and 122 magnetic point groups are not interchangeable.

example.title: Compare 2, 21′, and 2′
steps: The elements of 2 are {E,C₂}; it contains no time-reversal operation.
21′ is a gray magnetic point group with {E,C₂,Θ,ΘC₂}, totaling 4 elements.
2′ is a black-and-white  magnetic point group  containing {E,ΘC₂}; at the level of classical moment-vector actions it has only 2 elements.
For electron double groups, retain Ē as well; the classical element count of a magnetic point group cannot replace the count after a double-group lift.
example.result: Prime placement determines which operations are tied to time reversal; primes are not decoration.

lessons.pitfall: A gray  magnetic point group  may originate from a type-IV ordered  antiferromagnetic  structure. Seeing 1′ in its  point group  does not establish that the original  magnetic space group  contains pure  time reversal .

quiz.question: How are the 122 three-dimensional crystallographic magnetic point-group types composed?
quiz.explanation: 122=32 ordinary + 32 gray + 58 black-and-white types; the four-type count of 1651 concerns magnetic space groups.

quiz.question: What does type-IV  magnetic space group  antitranslation ΘT(τ) become when only point operations are retained?
quiz.explanation: Discarding translations removes T(τ) but retains its time-reversal marker. This is why a gray magnetic point group can still describe the macroscopic symmetry of some antiferromagnetic structures.

lessons.title: 14 Antiunitary multiplication and magnetic corepresentations
lessons.summary: Magnetic-group matrices must retain when complex conjugation is applied; traces of antiunitary parts cannot be interpreted freely as ordinary characters.
objectives: Use the left operation's type to decide whether to conjugate the right matrix
Calculate the square of a  antiunitary operator
Understand how corepresentations connect unitary-subgroup representations to their partners

sections.title: An operation consists of both a matrix and an antilinearity flag
paragraphs: Write operator 𝒟(g)=U_g K^εg, with εg=0 for unitary and εg=1 for antiunitary. Once the complete group and its lift are chosen, matrix-part multiplication follows directly from K U=U*K.

If the left operation is antiunitary, complex-conjugate the matrix of the right operation; two antiunitary operations multiply to a unitary one. After choosing space-group coset representatives, retain their additional lattice-translation phases and double-group lift signs consistently.
sections.formula: (U_gK^εg)(U_hK^εh)=U_g(U_h if εg=0; U_h* if εg=1)K^(εg+εh mod 2)

sections.title: A  corepresentation  is not simply another ordinary-character row
paragraphs: First find the irreducible representations of the unitary subgroup H, then examine how an antiunitary representative a maps each to its conjugate partner and how a² acts in that representation. Partners may be realized within the original space or require a larger space; these consistency relations determine whether pairing is necessary.

Under a basis change S, an antiunitary matrix part becomes S⁻¹U_aS*, not an ordinary similarity transform. Thus Tr(U_a) generally lacks ordinary characters' basis invariance. Inspect unitary characters, corepresentation type, and antiunitary multiplication checks first; do not insert every antiunitary matrix trace into ordinary group reduction formulas.

example.title: Why is (iK)² not −1?
steps: Take the one-dimensional operator A=iK. It acts on a complex number z as iz*.
A second application gives i(iz*)*=i(−i)z=z.
The matrix rule likewise gives U U*=i×(−i)=1.
Incorrectly using U² gives −1 and the false claim of a Kramers pair in one dimension.
example.result: Conjugation is structural in antiunitary multiplication; a one-dimensional antiunitary operator cannot square to −I.

lessons.pitfall: Distinguish ordinary complex-matrix multiplication, multiplication of the anti- unitary matrix  part, and phase multiplication of  little group  representatives. Do not omit K and continue interpreting the result as an ordinary representation.

quiz.question: For antiunitary A=UK and B=VK, what is the linear matrix of AB?
quiz.explanation: UKVK=UV*K²=UV*: the K on the left complex-conjugates V on the right.

quiz.question: For one-dimensional A=iK, what is A²?
quiz.explanation: iK iK=i(−i)K²=1. Omitting complex conjugation gives the incorrect −1.

lessons.title: 15 Θ×half-translation in  antiferromagnetic : where is pairing protected?
lessons.summary: Check both whether momentum returns to itself and the square of the combined operation, so a half-translation symmetry is not mistaken for degeneracy throughout the Brillouin zone.
objectives: Derive the square and Bloch phase of A=ΘT(τ)
Test whether −k and k are equivalent in magnetic  reciprocal lattice  coordinates
Distinguish protected pairing, symmetry permission and actual band results

sections.title: The square includes an actual lattice translation
paragraphs: Let A=ΘT(τ) be an actual antiunitary symmetry, with 2τ a unitary magnetic-lattice translation.  time reversal  commutes with real-space translations as operators, hence A²=Θ²T(2τ).

For spin 1/2, Θ²=−I; with this course’s active Bloch-phase convention, A² acts in the k subspace as −exp(−4πik·τ). References may use a different translation direction or exponential convention; check coordinates, τ and phases together.
sections.formula: A²|ₖ=−exp(−4πik·τ) I for spin 1/2; replace the initial − by + for spinless states

sections.title: A square of −1 also requires returning to the same k
paragraphs: The translation part of A does not change momentum, while Θ maps k to −k. It belongs to the magnetic little group of k only when −k=k+K, with K a magnetic reciprocal-lattice vector. Only if A²|ₖ=−I also holds does this symmetry alone directly imply same-k Kramers-type pairing.

A² can equal −I throughout a plane where the exponential is 1, but a generic k on that plane is still sent to a different −k. This does not establish twofold degeneracy at every k in the plane. Additional k-preserving operations such as PΘ require separate checks.

A²=+I only means this pairing argument does not apply. It does not exclude other representations, other symmetries, or accidental degeneracy. Symmetry alone also does not determine whether a material is a topological insulator.

example.title: τ=(0,0,1/2) in the magnetic unit cell
steps: Using fractional reciprocal coordinates of the magnetic cell, A²|ₖ=−exp(−2πik_z).
At Γ=(0,0,0), A preserves k and A²=−I, so pairing is protected.
At Z=(0,0,1/2), −Z is equivalent to Z, but A²=+I; A alone does not enforce pairing.
At k=(0.2,0,0), A²=−I, but A sends k to inequivalent (−0.2,0,0), linking spectra at two different momenta only.
example.result: An interactive demonstration should display both momentum return and the square's phase; checking only one misses a condition.

lessons.pitfall: τ is a half-translation relative to the magnetic cell. Using chemical-cell k coordinates or treating every k as a TRIM incorrectly locates the protected pairing.

quiz.question: For spin 1/2 and τ=(0,0,1/2), what is A² at k=(0,0,1/2)?
quiz.explanation: −exp(−2πi×1/2)=−(−1)=+1. A preserves this boundary momentum, but alone cannot enforce Kramers-type pairing.

quiz.question: For the same τ, A²=−I at k=(0.2,0,0). Why is A alone still insufficient to establish twofold degeneracy at this k?
choices: Because −I is not a valid operator
Because A maps k to inequivalent −k
quiz.explanation: Kramers-type pairing at the same k requires the antiunitary operation to preserve that momentum subspace; here its partner lies at a different −k.

lessons.title: 16 The double group of three-dimensional point group 222: why Q₈?
lessons.summary: Three ordinary twofold rotations commute, but lifting them to spinors leaves a central minus sign depending on multiplication order.
objectives: Write 222=D₂ and its eight-element  double group
Check the product of two twofold rotations with Pauli matrices
Distinguish linear representations, projective representations, and physical rotations

sections.title: First specify the spatial actions
paragraphs: D₂={E,C₂x,C₂y,C₂z} is the three-dimensional point group 222, with three mutually perpendicular twofold axes through a common origin. Its ordinary three-dimensional matrices satisfy C₂x C₂y=C₂y C₂x=C₂z. Here D₂ is the four-element rotation group, not the eight-element dihedral group of a square.

sections.title: Spinors retain information discarded by spatial matrices
paragraphs: Let X=−iσx, Y=−iσy, and Z=−iσz. Every lifted twofold rotation squares to −I, with XY=Z and YX=−Z. Together ±I,±X,±Y,±Z form quaternion group Q₈. Central element Ē=−I is invisible in spatial coordinates but cannot be omitted from spin-1/2 amplitudes.

sections.title: The projective minus sign comes from choosing a section
paragraphs: Choosing one lifted matrix per ordinary D₂ element can give D(g)D(h)=ω(g,h)D(gh), with ω=±1: a projective representation of the ordinary group. Restoring Ē makes the same matrices an ordinary linear representation of the double group. Different lift choices alter some ω values but cannot turn this noncommutative structure into D₂×C₂.

example.title: Compare XY with YX
steps: Applying the rightmost operation first, calculate (−iσx)(−iσy)=−iσz=Z.
Reversing order gives σyσx=−iσz, hence YX=+iσz=−Z.
After projection to three-dimensional rotations, both ±Z become C₂z, so ordinary  point group  still commute.
example.result: The central element Ē records the noncommutativity of Q₈; the geometric projection of the double group remains D₂.

lessons.pitfall: Double group means a double cover, not that every irreducible representation is two-dimensional or every level doubly degenerate.

quiz.question: In this lesson's convention, what is X²?
quiz.explanation: X=−iσx, so X²=(−i)²σx²=−I=Ē.

quiz.question: Why is D₂ commutative but its double group Q₈ noncommutative?
choices: Projection identifies ±Z as the same  spatial rotation
The rotation axes in three-dimensional space cease to be perpendicular
The double group changes atomic coordinates
quiz.explanation: The two orders differ only by a central minus sign, invisible under SO(3) projection.

lessons.title: 17 Double space groups: two sources of minus signs for a screw axis
lessons.summary: Retain separately the 2π spinor minus sign and the whole-cell translation Bloch phase, and specify the lifts of inversion and mirrors.
objectives: Derive the spin-1/2 eigenvalues of a 2₁ screw
Compare Γ with an axial zone boundary
Explain crystal  double group  conventions for inversion and mirrors

sections.title: Start with the three-dimensional screw operation
paragraphs: Take g={C₂z|(0,0,1/2)} in fractional coordinates. In the ordinary space group, g²=Tz. Its spin-1/2 lift ĝ also accumulates a 2π rotation, giving ĝ²=ĒTz. In an infinite crystal, wrapping plots into a cell does not make Tz the identity.

sections.title: Find eigenvalues along  screw axis
paragraphs: Discuss same-k eigenvalues only when g preserves the relevant k subspace. Along kz, use the active translation convention T(L)→exp(−2πik·L); solving the square relation gives λ±=±i exp(−iπkz). At Γ, λ=±i; at kz=1/2, λ=±1. Adjacent reciprocal periods can exchange the two labels, so they are not globally unique band names.

sections.title: Inversion is not a proper rotation in SU(2)
paragraphs: This lesson uses the standard electronic crystal  double group  convention:  spatial inversion  P commutes with lifted rotations and P²=E. P gives orbital parity without reversing spin direction. Mirror M=P C₂n then satisfies M̃²=Ē. Other Pin-cover conventions concern a different question and must be stated first; all improper transformations cannot simply be placed inside SU(2).

example.title: Evaluate the double-valued screw square at kz=1/2
steps: The translation phase is exp(−2πi×1/2)=−1.
The spin rotation contributes D(Ē)=−1.
The two factors multiply to +1, so the screw eigenvalues may be +1 or −1.
example.result: The double-valued screw squares to −1 at Γ and +1 at the axial boundary: the product of two explicit factors.

lessons.pitfall: A screw square of +1 does not itself establish degeneracy. Kramers pairing also requires specified antiunitary symmetry and its momentum action.

quiz.question: At kz=0, what are the spin-1/2 eigenvalues of ĝ?
quiz.explanation: The full-cell translation phase at Γ is 1, but the 2π spinor rotation still gives −1.

quiz.question: With the convention P²=E and P commuting with rotation lifts, what is the square of a mirror lift?
quiz.explanation: M̃=P C̃₂n, so M̃²=P² C̃₂n²=Ē.

lessons.title: 18 Color  point group : how do spatial operations induce color permutations?
lessons.summary: Use three colored vertices to extend “matching shapes” to “matching both shapes and labels.”
objectives: Write color symmetry as ordered pairs
Derive the permutation homomorphism from composition
Find the color-preserving kernel and identify its quotient

sections.title: Attach labels to symmetric objects
paragraphs: Colors here are finite-state labels representing orientations, decorations or interchangeable states. Label a triangle’s vertices red, green and blue counterclockwise. A geometric 120° rotation takes the red vertex to the original green position; a simultaneous uniform permutation red→green→blue→red restores the full colored pattern.

sections.title: The same permutation must act on all points of a given color
paragraphs: Write an operation as (R,π), acting by (r, c)→(Rr,π(c)), with AB applying B first. If each geometric symmetry determines a unique global color permutation, then ρ:G→Sₙ and ρ(gh)=ρ(g)ρ(h). Different red sites cannot arbitrarily acquire different target colors; that would not be a permutation of the color set.

sections.title: What questions do the kernel and image answer?
paragraphs: The color-preserving kernel H contains spatial operations that leave colors unchanged and is normal in G. The image imρ contains the color permutations actually present, which can be a small subgroup of Sₙ. In this lesson's C₃ rotation subgroup, the image is cyclic C₃ and the kernel is the identity. Including triangle mirrors requires separate checks; this experiment does not claim to exhaust that larger group.

example.title: Closure of a three-cycle
steps: Let r be a 120° rotation and π=(red green blue).
r³=E and π³=id, so (r,π)³=(E,id).
Its three powers induce three distinct permutations, so this C₃ subgroup's kernel contains only E.
example.result: The pattern’s C₃ color symmetry has three elements, but the pure spatial rotation r does not preserve each color label.

lessons.pitfall: Finite label permutations in crystallographic color groups differ from the continuous SU(3) color gauge group of QCD. Three colors do not automatically produce SU(3).

quiz.question: If π=(red green blue), where does π² send red?
quiz.explanation: First red→green, then green→blue; retain the composition order in the color part too.

quiz.question: Which operations belong to the kernel of ρ?
choices: An operation that moves no point
Spatial operations preserving every color label
quiz.explanation: Color preservation does not require fixing every point; nontrivial spatial operations can belong to the kernel.

lessons.title: 19 Three-dimensional color space groups: color and geometric periods
lessons.summary: Stack red, green, and blue layers along z, then extend periodically along three lattice directions.
objectives: Build a genuinely three-dimensional periodic colored model
Calculate powers of combined translations and the color-preserving translation kernel
Distinguish full translations from representatives modulo the cell

sections.title: The model extends periodically in three dimensions
paragraphs: Use three-dimensional cell vectors a,b,c and three sites on one x,y column at z=0,1/3,2/3, colored red, green, blue. Repeat the entire colored basis along a,b,c. To isolate the mechanism, the experiment checks only the specified translation generator and does not represent this simplified basis as a real ternary material.

sections.title: Shorter geometric period, longer color-preserving period
paragraphs: Ignoring colors, translation by c/3 makes the position set coincide. Retaining labels requires cycling the colors simultaneously. Let g=(T_(c/3),π); then g³=(T_c,id), where T_c is a color-preserving full-cell translation. In the chosen translation group, kerρ is generated by T_a, T_b and T_c, and the quotient is C₃.

sections.title: A finite display does not change group order
paragraphs: After wrapping at periodic boundaries, g³ appears to restore the initial image, but it actually sends every point to a neighboring unit cell in the same direction. The full color space group contains infinitely many translations; only the representatives modulo the chosen color-preserving translation subgroup form a three-element set. Changing the color-preserving cell requires updating coordinates, labels and the quotient description together.

example.title: What happens after the third operation?
steps: First application: z increases by 1/3 and red→green.
Second application: z increases by 2/3, and red→blue.
After three steps, z increases by 1 and the label returns to red; the atom is still in the neighboring cell.
example.result: Returning to the original color does not make the complete Seitz operation the identity; T_c remains.

lessons.pitfall: If colors represent different chemical elements, permitting label permutations is an extended formal symmetry; it does not automatically become a true symmetry of the Hamiltonian of a fixed chemical crystal.

quiz.question: What is the shortest positive color-preserving z translation in this model?
quiz.explanation: The shorter translation cycles colors; only c preserves all colors.

quiz.question: What is the order of the full operation g?
quiz.explanation: Every third power of g retains a nonzero full-cell translation, so g has no finite order in the complete infinite crystal.

lessons.title: 20 Black-and-white color groups and magnetic groups: matching labels do not imply identical operators
lessons.summary: Two colors help illustrate magnetic domains but cannot replace the antilinear action of time reversal.
objectives: Explain the two-color homomorphism and its index-two color-preserving kernel
Distinguish color exchange, moment reversal, and quantum time reversal
Explain the limits of color illustrations for  magnetic point group  and  magnetic space group

sections.title: Two-color permutations provide a language for group structure
paragraphs: For single-valued two-coloring with nontrivial exchange, the color image is C₂ and the color-preserving kernel H has index 2. Non-color-preserving operations lie in one coset gH. This explains certain black-and-white patterns and helps interpret primed/unprimed magnetic-group parts, but their physical actions still need separate definitions.

sections.title: Magnetic moments additionally have direction and odd time-reversal parity
paragraphs: A magnetic space operation (R,t,ε) acts on axial-vector moments as m′=(−1)^εdet(Rc)Rc m, with Rc an orthogonal Cartesian matrix. Merely swapping red and blue does not specify how a mirror rotates moments or how quantum states undergo complex conjugation. Pure time reversal in a gray magnetic group cannot generally be interpreted as a pure color swap of a fixed pattern that is everywhere nonzero and has a single color at each point.

sections.title: Test operators, not just two pictures
paragraphs: For spin 1/2, Θ may be −iσy K, with Θ²=−I. An ordinary two-label exchange matrix P instead satisfies P²=I and need not be antilinear. Although both can exchange ↑↔↓ in an arrow picture, they differ in complex amplitudes, multiplication, and pairing-theorem implications.

example.title: Assign different physical meanings to the same “color flip”
steps: In pure label space define P|red⟩=|blue⟩ and P|blue⟩=|red⟩, giving P²=I.
Defining Θ=−iσyK in the spin basis requires complex-conjugating the first application’s coefficients during the second application.
Directly calculate Θ²=(−iσy)(−iσy)*=−I.
example.result: A two-color exchange picture alone cannot determine the Kramers condition; specify the actual Hilbert-space operator.

lessons.pitfall: This section uses black-and-white patterns to explain structural connections; it does not identify all magnetic groups with ordinary finite color-permutation groups or infer band degeneracy from the number of colors.

quiz.question: If a nontrivial two-color homomorphism is onto C₂, what is its kernel's index?
quiz.explanation: The first isomorphism theorem gives G/kerρ≅C₂.

quiz.question: If a two-label swap obeys P²=I, does it follow that electronic Θ²=I?
choices: No; Θ additionally has antilinear and spinor actions
quiz.explanation: Electronic Θ² must be calculated using an antiunitary matrix and complex conjugation.

lessons.title: 21  spin point group : write the two rotations separately
lessons.summary: Let the lattice rotate by R and the spins by U, and directly test what moving positions and rotating arrows each accomplish.
objectives: Explain the two coordinate sets in [U∥R]
Test a combined symmetry with a two-site antiferromagnetic model
Distinguish spin space groups from Spin(3)

sections.title: Spatial and spin coordinates are distinct objects
paragraphs: Without SOC, exchange models allow spin and lattice directions to be considered separately. Write a spin-point operation as [U∥R]: R transforms positions and U transforms moments; U is an orthogonal matrix on moment components. Here U uses proper rotations, and the three-dimensional point-group examples use finite position sets with a common origin.

sections.title: Acting on only one part is usually not a symmetry
paragraphs: Take two identical sites at x=±a with moments +z and −z. Spatial C₂z exchanges sites but need not rotate +z spin into −z; spin C₂x reverses moments without moving sites. Only combined [C₂x∥C₂z] preserves this specified magnetic order. Disable spatial and spin parts separately to test the mechanism.

sections.title: Spin(3) and spin point groups answer different questions
paragraphs: Spin(3)≅SU(2) is the double cover of SO(3), explaining the electronic spinor's 2π minus sign. A spin point group specifies allowed pairings of independent spin and spatial operations for a magnetic structure. For spin-1/2 states, proper spin rotations can be lifted further to SU(2), but coincidence of classical arrows cannot reveal the lift's minus sign.

example.title: How two twofold rotations pair
steps: R=C₂z sends the +x site to the −x site.
U=C₂x sends this site's +z moment to −z.
The target site has moment −z, and the other site matches likewise.
example.result: The combination preserves this two-site magnetic order; moving sites alone or rotating arrows alone does not.

lessons.pitfall: Global spin-rotation symmetry of a Hamiltonian without SOC does not mean a chosen ordered domain preserves every global rotation. Distinguish the energy model from the stabilizer of a specific magnetic order.

quiz.question: In [U∥R], where do R and U act respectively?
choices: R acts on positions; U acts on moments
Both R and U must act on positions
quiz.explanation: Spin groups allow these two parts to be independent; test their paired action to establish structural invariance.

quiz.question: Are a spin point group and Spin(3)≅SU(2) the same concept?
choices: No; the former describes paired symmetries of a magnetic structure, while the latter is the double cover of rotations
Only when there are three sites
quiz.explanation: They may be related in electronic  subrepresentation , but have distinct definitions and roles.

lessons.title: 22 Spin space groups: half translation and a three-layer magnetic helix
lessons.summary: Include independent spin rotations in Seitz multiplication and check the complete three-dimensional periodic model, not merely a single chain.
objectives: Write the multiplication law for [U∥R|t]
Compare combined operations of an antiferromagnetic half translation and a three-layer helix
Distinguish spin-point projection from a pure-translation quotient

sections.title: The translation part still follows the Seitz rule
paragraphs: A three-dimensional spin-space operation [U∥R|t] sends positions to Rr+t and moments to Um. In composition, spin matrices multiply, while spatial translation must first be rotated by the outer R. The cell basis repeats along a,b,c and cross-cell translations are retained.

sections.title: Collinear half-translation and a coplanar three-layer helix
paragraphs: A collinear model places +z and −z moments at z=0 and 1/2; g=[C₂x∥E|c/2] preserves it and satisfies g²=[E∥E|c]. Another model places coplanar moments differing successively by 120° at z=0, 1/3 and 2/3; h=[C₃z∥E|c/3] satisfies h³=[E∥E|c]. These are classical-vector relations; an electron-spinor lift must also track the central minus sign after a full rotation.

sections.title: Do not lose the spin part when removing translation
paragraphs: Projecting [U∥R|t] onto [U∥R] gives the corresponding  spin point group  operation. A combined translation such as g projects to [C₂x∥E] rather than automatically disappearing. The kernel consists of pure translations with U=E and R=E. Discarding every operation with spatial R=E incorrectly deletes spin information.

example.title: The third step of the three-layer helical magnetic order
steps: Each step translates by c/3 and rotates moments through 120° in the xy plane.
After three applications the spin vector has rotated 360°, so U³=E.
The translation accumulates to c, leaving a full-cell translation that preserves the magnetic order.
example.result: h³ is a whole-cell translation, so the full h still has infinite order. The three cell pictures show only the cycle modulo translation.

lessons.pitfall: This lesson tests only specified generators and their powers. It does not assign a complete  spin space group  number to arbitrary materials or confuse  spin space group  classification with the 230 ordinary  space group  or 1651  magnetic space group  types.

quiz.question: For classical vectors, what is the square of g=[C₂x∥E|c/2]?
quiz.explanation: Spin C₂x squares to E; two half-translations add to c.

quiz.question: What results from projecting g into the spin point group?
quiz.explanation: Remove only t; retain the spin part.

lessons.title: 23 Collinear, coplanar and continuous spin-only stabilizers
lessons.summary: With every position fixed, which uniform spin operations still preserve every magnetic moment?
objectives: Find the spin-only stabilizer from the rank of the space spanned by moments
Distinguish proper SO(3) rotations from generalized O(3) spin operations
Explain why collinear magnetic order retains continuous symmetry

sections.title: The stabilizer must fix each magnetic moment individually
paragraphs: A spin-only operation [U∥E|0] exchanges no positions, requiring Umi=mi simultaneously at every site. Let W be the linear span of all moments. An orthogonal matrix fixing W pointwise can vary only on its orthogonal complement W⊥; this directly computes the stabilizer here.

sections.title: From one axis to all three dimensions
paragraphs: With no moments, rank W=0 and the stabilizer is O(3). Nonzero collinear order has rank 1, with a stabilizer isomorphic to O(2) inside O(3); its continuous proper-rotation part is SO(2) about the magnetic axis. Noncollinear coplanar order has rank 2, leaving only the identity and reflection in that plane. Noncoplanar order spanning three dimensions has rank 3, leaving only the identity.

sections.title: Improper spin matrices need a physical interpretation
paragraphs: Here U acts directly on time-odd magnetic moments. For detU=−1, write U=−V with V∈SO(3), corresponding to a proper spin rotation V plus  time reversal ; this part is antiunitary in the electronic Hilbert space. If only unitary proper rotations are permitted, collinear  stabilizer  is SO(2), whereas coplanar noncollinear and three-dimensional noncoplanar orders retain only the identity.

example.title: Three moments 120° apart in the xy plane
steps: Two nonparallel moments already span the xy plane, so rank W=2.
An orthogonal matrix fixing the xy plane pointwise can send its normal z only to ±z.
The two choices are E and diag(1,1,−1); the latter can be realized by combining Θ with a π rotation about z.
example.result: In the full O(3) description the stabilizer is a two-element mirror group; restricted to proper SO(3) rotations it is trivial.

lessons.pitfall: “Coplanar” here requires at least two noncollinear nonzero moments. If all arrows are actually collinear, their rank remains 1 even when drawn in a plane.

quiz.question: What is the continuous unitary spin-only part for nonzero collinear order?
quiz.explanation: Every rotation about the magnetic axis fixes all collinear moments individually.

quiz.question: Which nontrivial operation belongs to the O(3) stabilizer of noncollinear magnetic order in the xy plane?
quiz.explanation: The former fixes the plane pointwise; the latter generally reverses every in-plane moment.

lessons.title: 24 After including SOC: which  spin group  operations survive?
lessons.summary: Connect spin groups to magnetic groups through an explicit locking condition, and check structural symmetry and Hamiltonian symmetry separately.
objectives: Write the locking condition for embedding magnetic groups in spin space groups
Determine whether a combined operation survives under SOC
Do not infer degeneracy or magnetic-group type directly from zero net magnetization

sections.title: Independent and locked operations impose different constraints
paragraphs: The ideal model neglecting SOC permits independent U and Rc. In conventional magnetic groups, spin response is locked to spatial orthogonal Rc and the  time reversal  flag ε: U=(−1)^εdet(Rc)Rc. Selecting structure-preserving operations satisfying this relation gives corresponding magnetic-group operations; the actual Hamiltonian must also respect them.

sections.title: SOC can exclude an operation that is geometrically allowed
paragraphs: In the two-site model, [C₂x∥C₂z] preserves the arrows but fails U=±C₂z, so it generally lies outside the conventional magnetic point group. Likewise a half translation paired with C₂x can be a spin-space symmetry, whereas the same spatial translation permits only U=±I in a conventional magnetic space group. Another operation, [−I∥E|c/2], can reverse moments similarly in a collinear antiferromagnet, but includes time reversal and has a different quantum realization.

sections.title: What information is needed when starting from a material?
paragraphs: First specify the chemical elements, cell, moment directions and selected magnetic domain, then state whether SOC is negligible on the energy scale of interest. Collinear examples such as MnF₂ and NiO, along with coplanar noncollinear order, illustrate these distinctions, but actual domains, anisotropy and ligand positions require separate checks. Zero net magnetization alone neither establishes degeneracy of all bands nor automatically identifies a particular kind of altermagnetism.

example.title: Test the locking condition for [C₂x∥C₂z]
steps: In a common Cartesian basis write U=diag(1,−1,−1) and Rc=diag(−1,−1,1).
For ε=0, U=Rc is required, but the two differ.
For ε=1, U=−Rc=diag(1,1,−1) is required and still differs.
example.result: This combination may belong to the ideal model's  spin point group  but violates the SOC locking rule of conventional  magnetic point group .

lessons.pitfall: At finite SOC, spin groups are generally approximate symmetries relative to the energy scale of interest; some models may retain additional exact symmetries. Test the Hamiltonian rather than asserting that all such symmetries disappear.

quiz.question: For a pure spatial translation, which U are allowed in a conventional magnetic group?
quiz.explanation: Here Rc=I, so the locking condition becomes U=(−1)^εI.

quiz.question: If a magnetic structure is preserved by [U∥R|t], has this proved that its actual Hamiltonian with SOC preserves the operation?
choices: Yes; matching the pattern is sufficient
No; spin–space locking and the Hamiltonian must also be checked
It is enough for the moments to sum to zero
quiz.explanation: Structural matching is a necessary check, not a replacement for physical symmetry assumptions of the model.
